abstract.title: Objectives
abstract.p: This is a protocol for a Cochrane Review (intervention). The objectives are as follows:
The primary objective is to assess the benefits and harms of partial wrist fusion compared with placebo or sham surgery in adults with non‐inflammatory osteoarthritis of the wrist.

Secondary objectives are to assess the benefits and harms of surgery, including but not limited to, proximal row carpectomy, total wrist arthroplasty, and wrist denervation, compared with placebo or sham surgery, any non‐surgical intervention, or other type of surgery.

sec.p: Collection date 2026.

sec.title: Description of the condition
sec.p: Osteoarthritis is the most common form of arthritis and a leading cause of pain, functional limitation, and disability in older adults [1]. Estimates of the prevalence of wrist osteoarthritis vary widely because of differences in diagnostic criteria and study populations. Population‐based studies report prevalence rates of approximately 1.0% to 1.7% [2], while age‐stratified analysis suggests substantially higher prevalence in older adults, with radiographic wrist osteoarthritis reported in up to one‐third of individuals aged 75 to 79 years [3, 4, 5].

Wrist osteoarthritis most commonly develops secondary to prior trauma, particularly ligament injury or wrist fractures, although advancing age, abnormal wrist anatomy, obesity, and metabolic conditions such as gout or haemochromatosis (a genetic condition that leads to a build up of iron in the body), may also contribute [3, 4, 6, 7]. Several characteristic patterns of wrist osteoarthritis are recognised, including scapholunate advanced collapse (SLAC), a type of wrist osteoarthritis that results from chronic instability between the scaphoid and lunate bones, and scaphoid nonunion advanced collapse (SNAC), a type of wrist osteoarthritis that arises from an untreated or non‐healed scaphoid fracture [8, 9]. These patterns reflect underlying differences in disease aetiology and joint involvement, and contribute to clinical heterogeneity in presentation and management.

Diagnosis of wrist osteoarthritis is typically based on a combination of clinical features and imaging findings. Patients commonly present with wrist pain, stiffness, swelling, and reduced function, and examination may reveal tenderness, crepitus (a crackling or grinding sensation felt or heard during joint movement), and decreased range of motion. Radiographic features include joint space narrowing (decrease in the distance between the bones within a joint), subchondral sclerosis (densification of bone underlying articular cartilage), osteophyte formation (abnormal bone growth near the affected joint), and, in advanced cases, carpal collapse (loss of wrist bone alignment). The severity of radiographic changes does not always correlate with symptom severity, and radiographic patterns may be present in individuals with minimal symptoms.

The clinical course of wrist osteoarthritis is variable. Early symptoms are often intermittent and activity‐related, but pain may progress over time to become persistent and associated with functional impairment. Symptom patterns and progression differ between individuals and may depend on the underlying pattern of joint degeneration. This heterogeneity contributes to differences in treatment response and underpins the range of non‐surgical and surgical management options used in clinical practice. Early‐stage pain is often mild and intermittent, but symptoms often progress, leading to significant functional impairment and reduced quality of life [10]. As the disease progresses, pain may evolve from activity‐related mechanical discomfort to persistent, chronic pain associated with structural joint degeneration [11]. In addition, as the disease advances, people with wrist osteoarthritis may exhibit variability in symptom patterns, including differences in pain intensity, stiffness, and joint involvement [12]. These differences often reflect the specific pattern of joint degeneration (e.g. SLAC, SNAC, scaphotrapeziotrapezoid joint arthritis (STT), pancarpal osteoarthritis) and may influence both the clinical course and response to treatment [13]. Given the critical role of the wrist in daily tasks, even moderate impairment can disproportionately affect quality of life.

sec.title: Description of the intervention and how it might work
sec.p: Initial management of wrist osteoarthritis generally consists of non‐surgical treatments aimed at symptom relief. If symptoms persist despite conservative measures, surgical options are frequently considered [4].

sec.title: Non‐surgical management
sec.p: Non‐surgical management of wrist osteoarthritis includes wrist splinting, activity modification, nonsteroidal anti‐inflammatory drugs (NSAIDs), corticosteroid injections, and physical therapy [14]. These interventions primarily target pain reduction and inflammation but do not modify the underlying degenerative process [15].

Splinting and activity modification reduce mechanical stress across the wrist, potentially lessening symptoms during daily use [16]. NSAIDs and corticosteroid injections help modulate local inflammation and pain (nociceptive) signalling, offering temporary relief [17]. Physical therapy may improve range of motion, decrease stiffness, and enhance function by strengthening supporting musculature [18]. These approaches may delay surgical intervention, but they do not reverse structural degeneration and are generally used in earlier stages of disease or for patients with lower functional demands.

In addition, other injectable and biological treatments – such as platelet‐rich plasma, viscosupplementation (hyaluronic acid injections), hydrogels, stem cell‐based therapies, cartilage grafting techniques, and interposition arthroplasty using bioabsorbable scaffolds (inserting a soluble spacer in the joint) – have been explored in other synovial joints. However, current evidence does not support these interventions as effective disease‐modifying treatments, and their role in the treatment of wrist osteoarthritis remains unclear [19].

sec.title: Surgical management
sec.p: When symptoms persist despite conservative treatment, surgical options are often considered. These procedures aim to reduce pain and improve function by altering joint biomechanics, redistributing load, or removing sources of mechanical irritation.

list-item.p: Partial wrist fusion encompasses a group of procedures that aim to reduce pain while preserving some degree of wrist motion by selectively fusing specific carpal bones. The most common configuration is four‐corner fusion (4CF), which entails removal of the scaphoid and fusion of the capitate, lunate, hamate, and triquetrum [4]. This stabilises the midcarpal joint while preserving radiolunate motion, providing a balance between pain relief and functional mobility [20]. However, alternative fusion patterns are often employed based on the pattern of wrist osteoarthritis. These include three‐corner fusion (typically omitting the triquetrum), capitolunate fusion (a 'two‐corner' option, useful when osteoarthritis is confined to the radioscaphoid and midcarpal regions), and STT fusion, which is particularly relevant for isolated STT arthritis [21]. The choice of fusion technique is guided by joint involvement, cartilage preservation in adjacent joints, and the individual's functional demands.

Wrist arthrodesis (total wrist fusion) entails fusing the radiocarpal and midcarpal joints to eliminate motion and stabilise the bones of the wrist [22]. By eliminating the joint movement, it prevents mechanical irritation of thinned cartilage, resulting in pain relief. Arthrodesis is typically reserved for people with pan‐carpal arthritis or those with high functional demands who require a strong, stable wrist [23].

Proximal row carpectomy entails removal of the scaphoid, lunate, and triquetrum, facilitating direct contact between the capitate and the lunate fossa of the radius [24]. This creates a new biomechanical interface that redistributes load across preserved cartilage surfaces [25]. Pain is reduced by eliminating interactions at degenerated joint surfaces, while some motion is maintained, making it an option for selected individuals with preserved midcarpal integrity [26].

Total joint replacement entails implanting a prosthesis to replace damaged joint surfaces [27]. The goal is to preserve motion and reduce pain by restoring wrist alignment and facilitating low‐friction movement at the joints (articulation). Total joint replacement mimics natural wrist kinematics and may benefit patients with lower functional demands, but concerns about implant durability and complication rates have historically limited its widespread adoption. However, recent studies demonstrate encouraging mid‐ to long‐term outcomes. For instance, five‐year implant survival rates as high as 95% have been reported [28]. Nevertheless, survival rates can vary depending on implant type. For example, one prosthesis showed a five‐year survival rate of 84%, decreasing to 35% at 10 years [29].

Wrist denervation entails specifically interrupting the sensory nerve supply to the wrist joint to reduce pain perception without altering joint mechanics [30]. It is often considered in people with persistent pain but preserved motion who are poor candidates for more invasive procedures. While it may offer temporary symptom relief, it has been hypothesised that pain can recur as nerves regenerate.

sec.p: Each intervention – whether non‐surgical or surgical – resolves different aspects of the disease process, including pain, instability, and functional limitation. Their effectiveness likely depends on multiple factors, including the pattern and severity of joint degeneration, patient goals, activity level, and comorbidities.

sec.title: Why it is important to do this review
sec.p: Many people with wrist osteoarthritis, who do not experience adequate relief from non‐surgical measures, are eventually offered surgical treatment [4]. However, decisions about whether and when to escalate to surgery are often based on clinical judgment and preferences rather than high‐quality comparative data [31]. Clinicians currently lack a comprehensive and reliable synthesis of the evidence to guide decisions about when to escalate from non‐surgical to surgical management, and which surgical technique may offer the best outcomes.

Most existing systematic reviews focus narrowly on comparing proximal row carpectomy with 4CF – likely because these two procedures are commonly offered as alternatives to one another, making them more feasible for head‐to‐head randomised trials [32, 33, 34, 35, 36]. There is a notable scarcity of reviews comparing other surgical interventions, such as total wrist arthrodesis, wrist arthroplasty, or denervation [37, 38]. To our knowledge, no existing systematic review compares all major surgical approaches, or evaluates surgical versus non‐surgical treatments more broadly. This is in part caused by the heterogeneity of wrist arthritis, with different patterns of joint degeneration requiring distinct surgical approaches and making direct comparisons challenging. Nonetheless, a broader synthesis of available surgical and non‐surgical options could help guide clinical decision‐making and highlight important gaps in the evidence.

A 2018 systematic review attempted to assess the wider treatment landscape. It included only three randomised controlled trials – two comparing proximal row carpectomy with 4CF and one evaluating wrist splinting – and found no prospective studies that directly compared surgical and non‐surgical options [31]. It ultimately concluded that a substantial evidence gap remained and highlighted the need for high‐quality research to inform clinical decision‐making.

Wrist osteoarthritis affects more than one‐third of older adults, but treatment recommendations remain fragmented because of the absence of rigorous, inclusive evidence reviews [3, 4, 5]. Given this prevalence, and the range of available treatments, a comprehensive systematic review is both timely and necessary. This review will provide clearer guidance for clinicians, people with wrist osteoarthritis and policymakers, and identify gaps to inform future research. Furthermore, the findings of this review will improve shared decision‐making by facilitating patient understanding and assessment of surgical treatment options.

sec.title: Objectives
sec.p: The primary objective is to assess the benefits and harms of partial wrist fusion compared with placebo or sham surgery in adults with non‐inflammatory osteoarthritis of the wrist.

Secondary objectives are to assess the benefits and harms of surgery, including but not limited to, proximal row carpectomy, total wrist arthroplasty, and wrist denervation, compared with placebo or sham surgery, any non‐surgical intervention, or other type of surgery.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: We will follow the Methodological expectations for Cochrane intervention reviews (MECIR) when conducting the review [39], and PRISMA 2020 for the reporting [40].

sec.title: Criteria for considering studies for this review
Types of studies
sec.p: We will include randomised controlled trials (RCTs) of any design (e.g. parallel‐RCTs) and controlled clinical trials that use quasi‐randomised methods to allocate participants to study groups (e.g. date of birth or alternate allocation). We will include studies reported as full text, studies published as abstract only, and data from unpublished studies, where feasible. We will not use any language or publication date restrictions.

sec.title: Types of participants
sec.p: We will include participants aged 18 years and older with a diagnosis of symptomatic, non‐inflammatory osteoarthritis of the wrist, including isolated compartment involvement (e.g. STT joint osteoarthritis) or more extensive wrist osteoarthritis, diagnosed on the basis of clinical findings, imaging, or both.

We will exclude studies in which wrist pathology is attributed primarily to inflammatory arthritides (e.g. rheumatoid arthritis, psoriatic arthritis, or other systemic inflammatory joint diseases), as these conditions differ fundamentally from osteoarthritis in disease mechanism, clinical course, and treatment response.

We do not intend to distinguish whether degenerative wrist osteoarthritis has occurred 'as a consequence of' an inflammatory arthritis, as this cannot be reliably determined from published studies data. Rather, we will base our classification on how the study authors have defined the underlying wrist condition.

Studies that included mixed‐disease populations will be eligible if at least 80% of participants have non‐inflammatory wrist osteoarthritis, or if data for participants with osteoarthritis are reported separately.

sec.title: Surgery interventions
sec.p: We will include studies that evaluate any surgical intervention for wrist osteoarthritis. Studies will be eligible regardless of surgical technique, operative approach (e.g. arthroscopic or open), or perioperative protocol, provided that the intervention is intended to treat symptomatic wrist osteoarthritis.
Eligible surgical interventions may include, but are not limited to the following.

list-item.p: Partial wrist fusion (primary intervention of interest)
Total wrist fusion
Proximal row carpectomy
Total or partial joint replacement (wrist arthroplasty)
Wrist denervation

sec.p: We will exclude studies that compare different hardware types (e.g. one implant versus another) or minor technical or operative variations within the same surgical procedure (e.g. open versus arthroscopic fusion).

sec.title: Comparator interventions
sec.p: The planned primary comparator is placebo or sham surgery, defined as a procedure designed by study authors to mimic surgery while omitting the presumed therapeutic component. Examples include skin incision or arthroscopy without a therapeutic intervention, or simulated operative procedures performed under anaesthesia without corrective treatment.
Secondary comparators will include the following.

list-item.p: No treatment or usual care, such as no intervention, waiting list control, watchful waiting, or usual care not controlled by the study protocol. We will not classify structured therapeutic interventions as no treatment.

Non‐surgical management, including orthoses, intra‐articular injections, NSAIDs, structured physical therapy, or any combination of these. We will not exclude studies with non‐surgical comparators based on differences in dose, frequency, or duration of the intervention.
Other surgical procedures, in direct head‐to‐head comparisons (e.g. partial fusion versus proximal row carpectomy, or arthrodesis versus arthroplasty).

sec.p: Co‐interventions will be permitted. We will include studies in which co‐interventions are not applied equally across study arms but will consider them at increased risk of bias.

sec.title: Critical outcomes
sec.p: There is no core outcome set specifically for wrist osteoarthritis. The outcomes below reflect the main clinical domains and are informed by core outcome set development efforts in related musculoskeletal fields (e.g. International Consortium for Health Outcomes Measurement (ICHOM) [41] and Outcome Measures in Rheumatology (OMERACT) [42]), which prioritise pain, function, health‐related quality of life, and patient‐reported global assessments. Where studies report multiple outcome measures within a domain, we will prioritise outcomes according to the hierarchies specified below.

sec.title: Pain
sec.p: We will assess pain using the following hierarchy (in order of preference).

list-item.p: Wrist‐specific pain subscales from validated instruments (e.g. Patient‐Rated Wrist Evaluation (PRWE) pain subscale [43], Australian/Canadian Osteoarthritis Hand Index (AUSCAN) pain subscale [44], Modified Score for the Assessment and Quantification of Chronic Rheumatoid Affections of the Hands (M‐SACRAH) pain subscale [45]);
Generic pain intensity measures, including visual analogue scale (VAS) or numerical rating scale (NRS);
Other validated pain measures, as reported.

sec.title: Function
sec.p: We will assess function using the following hierarchy (in order of preference).

list-item.p: Wrist‐specific function subscales from validated instruments (e.g. PRWE function subscale, AUSCAN function subscale, M‐SACRAH function subscale, Functional Index for Hand Osteoarthritis (FIHOA) [46]);

Upper extremity–specific instruments, including the Michigan Hand Questionnaire (MHQ) function subscale [47], Disabilities of the Arm, Shoulder and Hand score (DASH) or Manchester‐modified DASH [48], Modern Activity Subjective Survey of 2007 (MASS07) [49], a measure of manual ability ‐ ABILHAND questionnaire [50], Patient‐reported Measure of Activity Performance of the Hand (MAP‐Hand) [51], Manual Ability Measure‐36 (MAM‐36) [52], or Upper Extremity Functional Index (UEFI‐15 or UEFI‐20) [53];
Perceived function measured using VAS or NRS scales.

sec.p: We will analyse pain and function domains separately where instruments provide validated domain‐specific subscales.

sec.title: Health‐related quality of life
sec.p: We will assess health‐related quality of life using generic instruments, prioritising mental health or overall health utility components where available, including the following, or other validated instruments as reported:

list-item.p: Short Form Health Survey mental health component (SF‐36);
EuroQol 5‐dimension instrument (EQ‐5D);
15‐Dimensional Health‐Related Quality of Life instrument (15D).

sec.p: Only the mental health or overall health utility components of generic health‐related quality‐of‐life instruments (e.g. SF‐36 mental health component, EQ‐5D index) will be analysed within the health‐related quality‐of‐life domain; physical function components will be analysed under the function domain.

sec.title: Patient‐reported global assessment of success
sec.p: We will measure patient‐reported global assessment of success (also referred to as global impression of success) as the proportion of participants who report improvement (e.g. 'much improved' or 'very much improved'), a good or excellent outcome, or other study‐defined global success measures, extracted preferentially as dichotomous outcomes. Where studies define global success using responder criteria (e.g. a prespecified percentage improvement in pain or function), we will accept these definitions provided they are clearly reported and applied consistently within the study.

sec.title: Rate of subsequent surgical intervention
sec.p: Subsequent surgical interventions will be any subsequent surgical procedure performed on the index wrist following the initial intervention, regardless of initial treatment allocation. We include subsequent surgical interventions as a critical outcome because they reflect treatment failure, complications, or disease progression following the index intervention, and provide a clinically relevant measure of harm across surgical and non‐surgical comparisons. We will compare the proportion of participants who undergo at least one subsequent surgical intervention between study groups, as reported. We will collect the data at the longest follow‐up available.

list-item.p: The proportion of participants who experience serious adverse events (e.g. deep infection, complex regional pain syndrome (CRPS), prosthesis removal, deep vein thrombosis, amputation, or death). We will collect the data at the longest follow‐up available.

The proportion of participants who experience any serious or non‐serious adverse event (e.g. superficial infection, wound dehiscence, hardware irritation, or tendonitis). We will collect the data at the longest follow‐up available.
Grip strength (measured by a hand‐held dynamometer in kg or lb, with lb values converted to kg prior to analysis)
Wrist range of motion (measured in degrees for flexion or extension and radial or ulnar deviation)

sec.title: Time points for evidence synthesis
sec.p: We will synthesise the evidence at three time points:

list-item.p: up to six months;
from six months to one year;
longer than one year.

sec.p: Where studies do not report outcomes at exactly the prespecified time points, we will extract data from the time point closest to each interval.

sec.title: Search methods for identification of studies
Electronic searches
sec.p: We will search the following databases:

list-item.p: Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials (CENTRAL; current year and issue) via Ovid EBM Reviews
MEDLINE via Ovid (from inception to the present)
Embase via Elsevier (Embase.com) (from inception to the present)

sec.p: In addition, we will search for ongoing or unpublished studies by consulting:

list-item.p: ClinicalTrials.gov, maintained by the US National Institutes of Health
WHO International Clinical Trials Registry Platform (ICTRP)
EU Clinical Trials Registry
Pan‐African Clinical Trials Registry

sec.p: We will search all databases from their inception to the present, without restrictions on language or publication status. We will use the Cochrane highly sensitive search filters designed to capture RCTs as described in Chapter 4 of the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Interventions [54]. Abstracts and full texts of potentially eligible studies that have been published in languages not spoken by the review team will be translated by professional translation services or by native speakers with relevant clinical or methodological expertise. Where feasible, outcome data and key methodological details will be verified by a second review author or a native speaker to ensure accuracy.
Full search strategies are provided in Supplementary material 1.

sec.title: Searching other resources
sec.p: We will examine the reference lists of included studies to identify additional relevant studies and published systematic reviews. Also, we will search for any errata or retractions of the included studies using PubMed (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/), and the Retraction Watch Database (https://retractiondatabase.org/), and will report the date we conducted this search.

sec.title: Selection of studies
sec.p: We will use Covidence for the study selection process [55]. We will use the Cochrane RCT Classifier integrated into Covidence to help prioritise records that are likely to be RCTs [56].

Two review authors (MS, BM) will independently screen the titles and abstracts of all records yielded by the search and identify any potentially eligible records. We will retrieve the full text of records that at least one review author judges as being potentially eligible. Two review authors (MS, BM) will independently screen the full‐text articles for eligibility and resolve any disagreements by discussion or by consulting a third review author (TK).

We will identify and exclude duplicate records and collate multiple reports of the same study under a single reference so that each study, rather than each report, is the unit of interest in the review. We will record the selection process in sufficient detail to complete a PRISMA flow diagram [40], and the 'Characteristics of excluded studies' table.

If included studies are missing relevant study details such as information regarding study design, measured outcomes, or numerical results, we will attempt to contact study authors in accordance with Chapter 5 of the Cochrane Handbook [57].

sec.title: Data extraction and management
sec.p: Pairs of review authors will independently extract data using a prepiloted data extraction form developed and tested on two studies identified during the search for this review. The review authors will resolve any discrepancies through discussion or adjudication by another review author (TK). For each included study we will record the following.

list-item.p: Study characteristics, including type (e.g. parallel), country, source of funding, and study registration status (with registration number recorded if available)
Participant characteristics at baseline, including age, sex, method of diagnosis of the disease or condition, duration of symptoms, and inclusion and exclusion criteria
Intervention characteristics, including details specific to each comparison.

For surgical interventions: we will extract the type of surgery (e.g. proximal row carpectomy, arthrodesis, arthroplasty), surgical approach (e.g. open versus arthroscopic), description of surgical technique, fixation or implant used (if applicable), setting (e.g. inpatient or outpatient), and use of postoperative rehabilitation or other co‐interventions.

For non‐surgical management (e.g. physical therapy, injections, medications): we will extract the type of treatment, dose or frequency (if applicable), treatment duration, delivery method (e.g. supervised versus unsupervised), and co‐interventions.
Outcomes reported, including the name of the measurement instrument used and its properties (including the scale and direction, e.g. 0 to 10, higher/lower is better) and timing of outcome assessments
Summary data for each outcome: number of events and number of participants per group for dichotomous outcomes, mean and standard deviation (SD) per group for continuous outcomes

sec.p: We will note in the 'Characteristics of included studies' if studies did not report outcome data in a usable way, and when we estimated or transformed data from a graph. We will resolve disagreements by consensus or by involving a third review author (TK). One review author will transfer data into the Review Manager (RevMan) file [58]. We will double‐check that data are entered correctly by comparing the data presented in the systematic review with the study reports.
We will use WebPlotDigitizer to extract data from graphs or figures if means and measures of variance are not reported in the text of included studies but can be extracted from the graphs [59].
If multiple outcome measures within the same domain are reported in a single study, we will extract data according to the prespecified outcome hierarchies described in the Outcome measures section.

For pain outcomes, we will prioritise wrist‐specific validated pain subscales (e.g. PRWE pain subscale, AUSCAN pain subscale), followed by generic pain intensity measures (VAS or NRS), and then other validated pain measures as reported.

For function outcomes, we will prioritise wrist‐specific validated function subscales (e.g. PRWE function subscale, AUSCAN function subscale), followed by upper‐extremity–specific instruments (e.g. MHQ, DASH), and then perceived function measured using VAS or NRS scales.

If studies report both final values and change‐from‐baseline values for the same outcome, we will extract final values. If studies report both unadjusted and adjusted values for the same outcome, we will extract adjusted values. If they analyse data based on an intention‐to‐treat (ITT) sample and another sample (e.g. per‐protocol, as‐treated), we will extract ITT values. If harms are reported at multiple time points, we will use the data from the one‐year follow‐up (primary time point of the review).

sec.title: Risk of bias assessment in included studies
sec.p: Two review authors will independently assess the risk of bias for each included study using the Cochrane Risk of bias tool (RoB 1) and the criteria outlined in the Cochrane Handbook [60]. We will resolve any disagreements through discussion or by involving another review author (TK). We will assess the following domains.

list-item.p: Selection bias: random sequence generation
Selection bias: allocation concealment
Performance bias: blinding of participants and care providers

Detection bias: blinding of the outcome assessor, assessed separately for self‐reported outcomes where the participant is the assessor and blinding of the assessor is necessary to minimise detection bias (e.g. pain, function, patient‐reported global assessment of success, adverse events) and assessor‐reported and more objective outcome measures (e.g. death, blood pressure) where blinding of the outcome assessor may not influence the measurement of the outcome
Attrition bias: incomplete outcome data
Selective outcome reporting bias: whether selective reporting of outcomes is present

Other biases, such as unequal application of co‐interventions across treatment groups, unit of analysis issues, and design‐specific issues. We will not exclude studies in which co‐interventions are not applied equally across study arms, but we will consider them at increased risk of bias.

sec.p: We will classify each potential source of bias as high, low, or unclear risk, with a justification for our judgement in the risk of bias table.
We will summarise the risk of bias judgements across different studies for each of the domains listed.

We will consider the impact of missing data on key outcomes. Where information on risk of bias relates to unpublished data, or correspondence with a study author, we will note this in the risk of bias table.
When considering treatment effects, we will take into account the risk of bias in the studies that contribute to that outcome.
We will present the graphs generated by the risk of bias tool to provide summary assessments of the risk of bias.

sec.title: Assessment of bias in conducting the systematic review
sec.p: We will conduct the review according to this published protocol and report any deviations from it in the 'Differences between protocol and review' section of the review.

sec.title: Measures of treatment effect
sec.p: We will present simple summary data for each intervention group (as visualised in forest plots).

list-item.p: For dichotomous outcomes: number of events and number of participants per group
For continuous outcomes: mean, SD, and number of participants per group

sec.p: We will use RevMan to perform data analysis [58].

We will analyse dichotomous outcomes (e.g. patient‐reported global assessment of success, adverse events, and serious adverse events) as risk ratios (RR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI). Subsequent surgical interventions will be treated as a dichotomous outcome where possible and analysed as the proportion of participants undergoing at least one subsequent surgical intervention using RR (95% CI). If studies report the relevant information as count or rate data (e.g. number of procedures per person‐time), we will analyse them using rate ratios, as recommended in Chapter 6 of the Cochrane Handbook [61]. If studies report time‐to‐event data, we will extract hazard ratios where available.

For continuous outcomes, we will use the mean difference (MD) when the same outcome is measured using the same scale across studies, or when outcomes can be meaningfully transformed to a common scale (e.g. rescaling pain scores from 0–10 to 0–100, or converting grip strength from lb to kg) with consistent direction of effect.

We will use the standardised mean difference (SMD) when studies measure the same underlying construct using different instruments that cannot be meaningfully rescaled to a common metric, such as health‐related quality of life or function assessed with heterogeneous questionnaires (e.g. SF‐36, EQ‐5D, Patient‐Reported Outcomes Measurement Information System (PROMIS)).

Where studies use SMDs, we will, when possible, re‐express the pooled effect on a familiar scale by multiplying the SMD by a representative baseline SD from the control group of a clinically representative study.
We anticipate using MD for outcomes such as pain or grip strength, and SMD for outcomes such as function and quality of life when reported using heterogeneous instruments (e.g. SF‐36, EQ‐5D, PROMIS).
Where available, we will use minimal important difference (MID) values to aid interpretation of the clinical relevance of effect sizes.

list-item.p: For pain, we will use an MID of 1.5 points on a 0 to 10 scale, consistent with published estimates for musculoskeletal conditions [62].
For health‐related quality of life, we will use an MID of 0.05 for the EQ‐5D index score, as reported in the PROMID database (www.promid.org) [63].
Where credible outcome‐ and population‐specific MID values are not available, we will interpret effect sizes based on the magnitude and precision of the estimates rather than applying a proxy MID.

sec.p: For each outcome, we will report the risks of events (for dichotomous data) or means (for continuous data) for all the intervention and comparison groups and the difference between groups in the summary of findings table.

For dichotomous outcomes, we will calculate the risk of events for the intervention and control group and the difference in the risks between the intervention and control group using GRADEpro GDT [64].

For continuous outcomes, we will estimate the control group risk using the mean value from a representative study (a combination of the most representative study population and a large weighting in the overall result in RevMan [58]).

sec.title: Unit of analysis issues
sec.p: For studies with more than two arms, we will describe all study groups in the 'Characteristics of included studies', but we will include only intervention groups that meet our review criteria in the analysis. When a study includes multiple relevant and similar treatment arms (e.g. two groups treated with different prostheses compared with fusion or non‐operative treatment), our preferred option is to combine the groups with different prosthesis into a single treatment group and to perform a single pairwise comparison, using methods described in the Cochrane Handbook [61]. If we do not wish to combine two different intervention groups into a single group (e.g. in a study that compares two different types of surgery and non‐operative treatment), and we are interested in assessing whether the type of surgery impacts the outcome in a single meta‐analysis, then we will halve the control group to avoid double‐counting [65].

sec.title: Dealing with missing data
sec.p: For dichotomous outcomes that measure benefits (patient‐reported global assessment of success), we will calculate the RR using the number of participants randomised to the group as the denominator. For dichotomous outcomes that assess possible harms of treatment (e.g. proportion of participants withdrawing because of adverse events), we will calculate the RR using the number of participants randomised to the group and receiving at least one treatment as the denominator.

For continuous outcomes (e.g. mean pain), we will calculate the MD or SMD based on the number of participants analysed at the time point. If the number of participants analysed was not presented for each time point, we will use the number of randomised participants in each group at baseline.

Where possible, we will compute missing SDs from other statistics, such as standard errors, CIs or P values, according to the methods recommended in the Cochrane Handbook [61]. If we cannot calculate SDs, we will impute them from other studies in the same meta‐analysis [61].

sec.title: Reporting bias assessment
sec.p: To assess small‐study effects, we plan to generate funnel plots for meta‐analyses that include at least 10 studies of varying size. If we detect asymmetry in the funnel plot, we plan to review the characteristics of the studies to assess whether the asymmetry was likely because of publication bias or other factors, such as the methodological or clinical diversity of the studies. Where we are able to pool more than 10 studies, we will conduct formal statistical tests to investigate funnel plot asymmetry, and follow the recommendations in Chapter 13 of the Cochrane Handbook [66].

To assess outcome reporting bias, we will check study protocols against published reports. For studies published after 1 July 2005, we will search the Clinical Trials Register at the International Clinical Trials Registry Platform of the World Health Organization (www.who.int/clinical‐trials‐registry‐platform) for the study protocol. If study protocols are unavailable, we will compare the outcomes reported in the methods and results sections of the study reports.

sec.title: Primary comparison
sec.p: For the primary analysis, we will pool studies that evaluate partial wrist fusion compared with placebo or sham surgery. If we do not identify any placebo‐controlled studies, subsequent primary comparisons will include partial wrist fusion compared with:

list-item.p: no treatment or usual care;
non‐surgical management.

sec.p: We will combine different partial wrist fusion techniques into a single intervention group within each comparison.

If both placebo‐controlled and no treatment‐ or usual care–controlled studies are available, the primary analysis will include only placebo comparisons. That is, we will synthesise them separately as two meta‐analyses:

list-item.p: partial wrist fusion versus placebo surgery, and
partial wrist fusion versus no treatment or usual care.

sec.p: However, we will also conduct a sensitivity analysis in which we pool placebo and no treatment or usual care comparators within a single meta‐analysis.

sec.title: Secondary comparisons
sec.p: In secondary analyses, we will pool studies that evaluate other surgical procedures (e.g. proximal row carpectomy, total wrist arthroplasty, wrist denervation, total wrist fusion, or other procedures identified in the literature) compared with:

list-item.p: placebo surgery;
no treatment or usual care;
non‐surgical management;
other surgical procedures (direct head‐to‐head comparisons).

sec.p: We will not combine different surgical procedures within a single comparison but will analyse them separately.

sec.title: Meta‐analysis of numerical data
sec.p: Before pooling the data, we will assess the clinical and methodological diversity of the included studies in terms of participants, interventions, outcomes and study characteristics to determine whether a meta‐analysis is appropriate. We will then group studies according to the predefined primary and secondary comparisons described above, and present results for each outcome. Within each comparison, we will pool data from studies with sufficiently similar populations, interventions, comparators, outcomes, and follow‐up durations. We will display pooled estimates using forest plots.

We plan to synthesise effect estimates using a random‐effects meta‐analysis model, based on the assumption that clinical diversity is likely to exist, and that different studies are estimating different intervention effects. We will use the Restricted Maximum Likelihood (REML) estimator to estimate between‐study variance, and the Hartung‐Knapp‐Sidik‐Jonkman method to calculate a confidence interval for the meta‐analysis effect estimate when there are at least three studies, and the estimate of heterogeneity is greater than zero. In other scenarios (i.e. in pooled analyses of two studies, or where the estimate of heterogeneity is equal to zero) we will use the Wald‐type method. If interventions and outcomes are too dissimilar to be included in a meta‐analysis, we will present effect estimates and 95% CIs of each study in forest plots (displaying individual study results without pooling), and summarise the results in the text.

sec.title: Investigation of heterogeneity and subgroup analysis
sec.p: We will assess statistical heterogeneity by visually inspecting forest plots to check for obvious differences in results between the studies, and by using the I² [67], and Chi² tests [68].
As recommended in the Cochrane Handbook, we will interpret an I² statistic for heterogeneity as follows:

list-item.p: 0% to 40% might not be important;
30% to 60% may represent moderate heterogeneity;
50% to 90% may represent substantial heterogeneity; and
75% to 100% represents considerable heterogeneity [68].

sec.p: We will keep in mind that the importance of the I² statistic depends on the magnitude and direction of effects, and the strength of evidence for heterogeneity. We will interpret a P value of 0.10 or lower on the Chi² test as evidence of statistical heterogeneity.
Where we identify substantial heterogeneity, we will report it and investigate possible causes by following the recommendations in Chapter 10 of the Cochrane Handbook [68].

We are not planning to carry out formal hypothesis‐testing subgroup analyses at this stage. However, we prespecify the following exploratory subgroup analyses, which we will conduct only if substantial clinical or statistical heterogeneity is observed in pooled analyses.

list-item.p: Variation within the surgical procedure (e.g. different modifications of partial wrist fusion or proximal row carpectomy, such as open versus arthroscopic; or different fixation method)
Variation in the non‐surgical management (e.g. varying doses or regimens of splinting, glucocorticoid injection, other conservative management)
Variation in the type of osteoarthritis (post‐traumatic versus idiopathic)

sec.p: We specified these subgroup categories based on known potential differences in mechanism of action, invasiveness, and expected clinical effects of different surgical procedures, as well as differences in intensity and mechanism of nonsurgical comparators, as outlined in the Background and reflected in the PICO (patient, intervention, comparison, outcome) framework. We will consider all subgroup analyses to be exploratory, we will interpret them cautiously, and will use them to generate hypotheses rather than to draw definitive conclusions. Where we conduct subgroup analyses, we will formally assess differences between subgroups using the random‐effects meta‐regression implemented in RevMan, and will interpret interaction tests cautiously in accordance with guidance in the Cochrane Handbook [68].

sec.title: Equity‐related assessment
sec.p: We considered undertaking a formal equity‐focused assessment in line with Chapter 16 of the Cochrane Handbook [65]. However, based on the anticipated limited and inconsistent reporting of equity‐relevant characteristics (e.g. socioeconomic status, race or ethnicity, and other PROGRESS‐Plus factors, which describe characteristics associated with differences in health opportunities and outcomes [69]) in surgical studies for wrist osteoarthritis, we do not plan a formal equity analysis. Where available, we will extract and report participant and setting characteristics (e.g. age, sex, country, and healthcare setting) and consider their implications for the applicability and generalisability of the review findings.

sec.title: Sensitivity analysis
sec.p: We will conduct the following sensitivity analyses to investigate the robustness of the outcomes (pain and function) to potential selection and detection biases. We will conduct sensitivity analyses for the primary comparison only.

list-item.p: Selection bias: we will remove the studies that report inadequate or unclear allocation concealment from the meta‐analysis to assess the impact on the overall treatment effect.
Detection bias: we will remove the studies that report inadequate or unclear participant blinding from the meta‐analysis, to assess the impact on the overall treatment effect.

sec.title: Certainty of the evidence assessment
sec.p: We will create a summary of findings table using the following outcomes: pain, function, health‐related quality of life, patient‐reported global assessment of success, rate of subsequent surgical intervention, adverse events, and serious adverse events. If multiple outcome measures are reported within a domain, we will prioritise measures in the hierarchical order listed in the Critical outcomes. The primary time point for each outcome will be one year.

The primary summary of findings table will be partial wrist fusion versus placebo surgery. If no data are available to address this comparison, the summary of findings table will instead present the comparison between partial wrist fusion and no treatment or usual care.

We may prepare additional summary of findings tables for other surgical procedures if we identify studies that compare surgery with placebo, no treatment or usual care, or non‐surgical management. We will present comparisons between different surgical procedures in additional summary of findings tables only if objectives involving placebo surgery, no treatment or usual care, or non‐surgical management cannot be addressed with the available data, and we judge the comparisons to be of substantial clinical relevance.

Two review authors (MS, TK) will independently assess the certainty of the evidence, with disagreements resolved by discussion or by involving a third review author. We will use the five GRADE considerations (study limitations (overall risk of bias), consistency of effect, imprecision, indirectness and publication bias) to assess the certainty of a body of evidence as it relates to the studies that contribute data to the analyses for the prespecified outcomes, and report the certainty of evidence as high, moderate, low, or very low. We will justify, document and incorporate judgements into reporting of results for each outcome.

We will use GRADEpro GDT software to prepare the summary of findings tables [64]. We will use version 3 of the GRADEPro GDT view to display our summary of findings tables, which has the 'What happens' column. We will justify all decisions to downgrade the certainty of evidence for each outcome using footnotes, and we will make comments to aid the reader's understanding of the review where necessary.

sec.title: Consumer involvement
sec.p: We did not involve consumers in developing this protocol because of limited resources. However, we used preliminary OMERACT hand osteoarthritis core outcome sets (as appropriate, given that the main interest of this review is the wrist joint) to inform the review's outcomes, which have been developed with consumer involvement. Additionally, we will evaluate opportunities to include patient partners in the later stages of the review process (e.g. interpretation of findings and dissemination).
